html:
A famine that struck northern Europe from 1315 to 1317, after years of cold and endless rain ruined the harvests. Millions died, and some towns lost a tenth of their people or more.

The spring of 1315 was so wet that fields could not be sown, and the grain that did grow rotted. 1316 was as bad. Wheat prices rose many times over. People ate their seed grain, their draft animals and even bark, and chroniclers reported cannibalism. Even King Edward II of England found no bread for his household on one journey. Cattle plague then killed many of the herds that were left.

Europe's population had grown for three centuries, farming poor land at the edge of what could feed it. The famine ended that long boom. It came at the start of the Little Ice Age, a cooler period. Thirty years later the Black Death struck a weakened people and killed a third or more of Europe. Some link the story of Hansel and Gretel to memories of these years.
sum: A famine that struck northern Europe from 1315 to 1317, after years of cold and endless rain ruined the harvests. Millions died, and some towns lost a tenth of their people or more.
